rv.q: Receiving its superb British premiere now at the Old Vic, Bess Wohl’s play is a consummately clever and insightful piece about the frightening psychological appeal of fascism.
Director Katy Rudd zeroes in on the script’s abundant opportunities for situational comedy, and much of the show ends up being deeply funny despite its ominous tone.
Wohl’s play is a fine example of both.
But on the whole it is coolly, queasily hypnotic.
But after all the careful scene-setting, the writing loses its grip.
The storytelling is ingenious and well-paced, and the depth and subtlety of the characters provide constant surprises.
A stealthily powerful play gets the production of its dreams in Camp Siegfried, which marks a high-profile UK presence for the American writer Bess Wohl.
Katy Rudd’s direction ensures that this personal story is as much about now as about history.
Ultimately, despite its many felicities, as the evening progresses you realize you're never in doubt about what the author wants you to think.
The play is however served by a nigh-on faultless production.
There’s an eerie beauty to Katy Rudd’s production, the simple but effective set design by Rosanna Vize, the film footage from the real camp, and Rachel-Leah Hosker’s mesmerising choreography.
Camp Siegfried is 1 of the most outstanding pieces of new writing we’ve seen this year and it’s absolutely thrilling to see it brought to life by such a talented young acting pairing.

cn.t: Critics praise this gripping two-hander about teens seduced by Nazi ideology at a 1930s Long Island camp as stealthily powerful and disturbingly pertinent, with strong performances elevating Wohl's exploration of fascism's insidious appeal.
